blocks.content: The previous module covered normalization, shaping a schema to minimize redundancy, this new module, Indexing, covers a different concern entirely, how a database makes queries against that schema fast, even as a table grows to millions of rows.
This topic covers what actually happens without an index, the classic book index analogy, and the real cost every index adds, setting up the specific index types covered in the rest of this module.

Without an index, finding rows matching a WHERE condition requires the database to check every single row in the table one by one, called a full table scan, on a small table this is fast enough to not notice, on a table with millions of rows, it becomes genuinely slow.

A database index works exactly like the index at the back of a textbook, without it, finding every mention of a topic means reading the entire book page by page, with it, you jump directly to the right pages, a database index gives the same shortcut for finding rows matching a specific value.

An index is a separate structure storing the indexed column values in sorted order, alongside a pointer to where the full row actually lives in the table, this sorted structure is what lets the database use fast search techniques instead of checking every row.

On a table with one million rows, a query without a useful index might need to check all one million rows in the worst case, the same query using an index on the filtered column typically needs only a handful of comparisons, the difference in practice is often the gap between a query taking milliseconds versus seconds.

An index speeds up reads, but every write, an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, now has to keep that index up to date as well as the table itself, a table with many indexes pays this cost on every single write, this tradeoff is covered in depth in the later Index Tradeoffs topic.

blocks.title: This is the same read versus write tradeoff seen with denormalization
blocks.content: Adding an index and denormalizing a schema, covered in the previous module, both trade write cost for read speed, they are different mechanisms solving a related underlying tension between fast reads and cheap writes.

A good index candidate is a column frequently used in a WHERE clause, a JOIN condition, or an ORDER BY, exactly the columns queries actually filter, join, or sort on, indexing a column that queries almost never reference adds write overhead with little corresponding read benefit.

blocks.title: Not every column deserves an index
blocks.content: A table with an index on every single column pays the full write overhead cost repeatedly while gaining meaningful benefit from only a few of those indexes, deliberate, selective indexing tends to outperform indexing everything.
